subtype: Approach: groups similar homework into one session [Action]
passage:
Dear Himani,

Guess what changed my evenings? Last week I bounced from history reading to maths to history writing to English reading, and after two hours I had barely done a thing. My pencil kept going missing and I kept losing my place. So on Monday I tried something different: first all the reading tasks in a row (the history chapter, the English poem, my science notes), thirty-five minutes. Then a short break. Then all the writing: history answers, an English paragraph, the lab record. It took one hour forty minutes and I finished before dinner. Switching costs me more than I thought. Try it and tell me if it works for you too.

Tushar

qa.q: How long did the reading block last?
qa.a: The reading block took thirty-five minutes.

qa.q: How did Tushar feel about the old way of working?
qa.a: Tushar felt frustrated, having done little in two hours and lost the place again and again.

qa.q: What could Tushar do if the writing block feels too long?
qa.a: Tushar could split it into two short parts with a stretch between, keeping similar tasks together.

qa.q: How might Himani see Tushar's tip?
qa.a: Himani might be curious and glad to test whether it works for Himani's own study.

grounding: Shows a student grouping all reading tasks and then all writing tasks into separate sessions to avoid switching.
